topic.title: Stochastic Gradient Dynamics and Convergence
topic.overview: Stochastic gradient descent uses noisy local information to optimize large objectives. This topic examines learning-rate schedules, stability, noise, implicit bias, and convergence under assumptions closer to practical training. The path taken by optimization matters as well as the objective eventually reached.
topic.whyItMatters: Classical bounded-gradient or smoothness assumptions can fail in common models. Understanding when noise helps escape unstable points and when it causes divergence supports more reliable training choices rather than treating one schedule as universally appropriate.
topic.evolution: The collection includes 1990s learning-rate schedules and diffusion approximations. Later theory relaxes bounded-gradient assumptions and examines asynchronous updates, large steps, and overparameterized problems. Recent taming schemes handle broader gradient growth and prove saddle avoidance under specified conditions. These results concern different regimes and do not collectively guarantee global optimization of arbitrary neural losses.
openQuestions: Which measurable training signals can identify the appropriate convergence regime?
How do stochastic implicit biases change with batch size and adaptive step geometry?
